canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: When organizational members collectively value the change (change valence) and share a favorable appraisal of task demands, resources, and situational support (change efficacy), the result is change commitment — the shared resolve to initiate, persist in, and cooperate on implementation.

sentences.text: Collective organisational change readiness is a shared psychological state rather than an individual attitude or a stock of resources.

It has two components that together produce change commitment, the collective resolve to pursue implementation: members must collectively value the change as worthwhile — their individual reasons may differ without weakening that shared valuation — and they must share a favourable appraisal of what implementation will demand, whether resources suffice and whether circumstances support it.
Capacity is an input to that appraisal rather than the readiness itself, since identical resources yield different implementation outcomes depending on how members judge them.
Where readiness is weak, initiatives are described as fragmenting and proving short-lived irrespective of the digital competence available.

canonicalConditions.label: Structured change management & change communication
canonicalConditions.definition: Change narratives, cascading sponsorship, frame-of-reference communication, and momentum-building decomposition as the delivery mechanism of change readiness.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Structured change management — change narratives, cascading sponsorship, frame-of-reference communication, momentum-building decomposition — delivers change readiness.

sentences.text: Structured change management translates transformation intent into practices that help people understand, judge and take part in the change.
A credible narrative connects the target state to human and institutional concerns rather than describing the architecture alone.
Sponsorship is distributed across levels so that stakeholder groups discuss the change with leaders they trust instead of receiving relayed messages.
Communication runs both ways and is tailored to each group's frame of reference, including the emotional uncertainty that project and agile routines leave unaddressed.
For large programmes, short time-boxed cycles on pain points surfaced in regular cross-departmental workshops create visible progress and learning.
Together these support change readiness; they do not by themselves produce it.

matrix.label: Assessment & Feedback
matrix.definition: Conditions that make readiness and maturity assessment multidimensional, valid, actionable, and iterative through action and reassessment.

canonicalConditions.label: Multi-dimensional readiness/maturity assessment architecture
canonicalConditions.definition: Readiness/maturity assessed across validated multi-dimensional structures with staged levels, dimension-level (not only aggregate) evaluation, and hard+soft+context domains.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: A validated multidimensional assessment architecture — staged levels, dimension-level rather than aggregate-only evaluation, hard, soft, and contextual domains, and the strategic need judged separately from the readiness to change — makes readiness and specific gaps visible so they can be prioritized and acted on.

sentences.text: A multi-dimensional readiness and maturity assessment architecture evaluates transformation readiness across several distinct domains and reports per dimension rather than as a single index.

The evidence is largely prescriptive about construction: per-dimension scoring keeps visible the bottlenecks a composite score hides, and strength on infrastructure or leadership is no proxy for organisational integration.

Coverage must reach beyond structure and process to the soft dimensions governance instruments habitually omit, and target states follow sector, size and strategy rather than defaulting to the highest level.
The strategic need for change is judged separately from the capability to execute it, and current and future capability are graded separately within each dimension rather than blended into one score.
Where one scale would conflate distinct capabilities, parallel scales are used, and an instrument's domain coverage is cross-checked before it is adopted.
The limits are documented as consistently as the design guidance, since the field has not converged on a consensual maturity model applicable across sectors.
Coverage also stays uneven: business-model dimensions are barely addressed, layer coverage is incomplete, and organisations score highest on technology while process, goals and boundaries lag.
An instrument is finally a socio-technical artifact whose usefulness depends on the organisation around it, and maturity models fail to steer transformation where that system is ignored.

canonicalConditions.label: Assessment validity & multi-perspective measurement
canonicalConditions.definition: Valid measurement through multi-assessor panels, employee-vs-leadership triangulation, validated instruments, and interview-corrected self-assessment.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Assessment validity is secured through multi-assessor panels, employee-versus-leadership triangulation, and validated instruments, producing readiness signals decisions can trust; single-source self-assessment is unreliable specifically for perception-gap-prone dimensions (soft-governance, leadership-versus-frontline), where triangulation is what exposes the divergence.

sentences.text: Assessment validity concerns whether a readiness signal can be trusted enough to act on.

Its central device is triangulation across perspectives, because employees and leadership perceive foundational readiness — strategy clarity, market awareness, culture — differently, and the size of that gap is itself treated as a risk signal.

The gap follows role: strategy and vision are rated less favourably by academic and consulting respondents and infrastructure less favourably by technical ones, so results are disaggregated by role rather than pooled.
Single-source self-assessment is therefore weakest exactly where the gap matters most, and leadership estimates need checking against frontline experience.

Instrument quality forms a second strand, since reliability established in one sector and language confirms internal consistency there rather than portability, so factor structures are re-established locally before being relied on.

Semantic ambiguity survives design iteration — ambiguous statements persisted through repeated redesign cycles — which is why an instrument is piloted with structured interviews rather than assumed to be read as intended.

canonicalConditions.label: Assessment-to-action linkage
canonicalConditions.definition: Converting assessment into action: KPIs, thresholds, recommendation engines, roadmaps, continuous reassessment procedures, and accessible self-service tooling.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Assessment results are systematically converted into action via KPIs, thresholds, recommendations, roadmaps, and continuous reassessment — assessment is never an end in itself.

sentences.text: Assessment-to-action linkage is the requirement that an assessment ends in a decision rather than a report.

Reassessment intervals and progress thresholds are fixed in advance, before rollout, so correction is triggered by design rather than by visible failure, which also counters the reluctance to abandon sunk commitments.
What is tracked matters as much as when: intermediate, digitally specific measures show how the activity system is performing, where traditional outcome metrics only report after the fact.
Indicator sets are weighted to context rather than applied uniformly, and a human review step catches the anomalies that the data alone would carry forward.
Access belongs to the linkage too, since a self-administrable, freely available assessment removes the barrier that keeps resource-constrained organisations from ever reaching a result to act on.

canonicalConditions.label: Readiness as distinct construct from maturity
canonicalConditions.definition: Readiness (behaviors, willingness, cyclical system) formally distinguished from maturity (implementation status) as an assessment precondition.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Transformation readiness — behaviours, willingness, and a cyclical capacity to change — is assessed as a construct distinct from maturity (attained implementation status), so that assessment captures the disposition and ability to change rather than only the state already reached.

sentences.text: Readiness and maturity are distinct constructs, and the framework keeps them apart deliberately.

Maturity records how far an implementation has progressed, readiness whether the organisation has internalised the behaviours needed to draw value from it — so technical maturity cannot be read as evidence of behavioural readiness, and the two are assessed as non-substitutable constructs rather than merged into one score.

Organisational readiness is also not simply the older e-readiness and digital-readiness tradition, which is overwhelmingly governmental and institutional in focus and has yet to settle a unified definition of the transformation-specific construct.
Because a successful transformation changes the environment that prompted it, readiness is reassessed against competitive conditions and not only against internal capability.

matrix.label: External Context & Constraints
matrix.definition: External conditions concerning enterprise scale and resource constraints and sectoral, regional, and institutional contingency.

canonicalConditions.label: SME resource & capability constraints
canonicalConditions.definition: SME resource, skill, and R&D constraints with substitution mechanisms (intermediaries, collaboration) and SME-adapted models instead of scaled-down large-firm approaches.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Framework application is calibrated to small- and medium-sized-enterprise resource and capability constraints; where gaps exist, intermediaries, collaboration, and adapted models provide feasible substitution mechanisms.

sentences.text: SME resource and capability constraints denote the budget, skill and development capacity that bound what transformation is feasible in a smaller enterprise.

This is not a scaled-down large-firm case: preparatory customisation that bigger organisations absorb through dedicated functions falls to the SME itself, and maturity models premised on resource slack set targets it cannot act on.
Barriers compound, because short-term orientation and an absent digital strategy inside the firm meet an ecosystem that itself lacks the capacity to spot and scale opportunities.
Readiness is asymmetric: cultural and strategic dimensions, movable by internal effort, run ahead of the analytical and technical ones that need capital and scarce skills.
Substitution is the practical answer — collaboration with partners and research institutions, and intermediaries supplying missing networks and expertise.
Assessment therefore begins from the resources actually present and calibrates to firm size rather than an absolute transformed state.
Size is not uniformly decisive: where infrastructure investment was examined directly, it weighed less than the constraint literature implies.

canonicalConditions.label: Sectoral, regional & institutional contingency
canonicalConditions.definition: Transformation approaches conditioned by sector, region, regulation, and institutional context; uniform strategies and imported models underperform.
canonicalConditions.enabling_statement: Transformation approaches are calibrated to sector, region, regulation, and institutional context — uniform strategies and imported models are expected to underperform.

sentences.text: Sectoral, regional and institutional conditions shape how far a transformation approach or assessment instrument transfers without adaptation.

Methods carry the assumptions of the setting they were built in: a federated architecture may depend on collaboration that is not yet established, while a commercial maturity model measures objectives that do not fit a public-service mission.
Assessment instruments likewise presume infrastructure access and digital literacy that cannot be taken for granted everywhere.
Context can also reverse an apparent enabler, since in data-sensitive industries organisation-wide accessibility and sharing with competitors become compliance risks rather than benefits.

External pressure from customers, competitors and regulators creates urgency without supplying the capacity to respond, so pressure and readiness are assessed separately; in some sectors policy and regulation are weighted more heavily than technology itself.
Framework application therefore tests its contextual assumptions explicitly, including local infrastructure and literacy baselines, before a nationally designed reform is scaled outwards.

registers.title: Technology-first transformation without organizational alignment
registers.body: Grassroots or infrastructure-only investment stalls ROI when organizational, governance, and business-model alignment are missing.

registers.title: Waterfall, IT-centric EA in digital contexts
registers.body: Traditional document-driven, IT-focused EA practice is structurally mismatched with agile, business-focused, ecosystem-oriented transformation demands.

registers.title: Framework worship
registers.body: Treating explanatory frameworks as prescriptive methodologies and enforcing rigid compliance produces disappointing outcomes; capability can exist without named frameworks.

registers.title: One-size-fits-all governance and maturity models
registers.body: Uniform governance designs, scaled-down large-firm models, unweighted indicator panels, and directly transplanted commercial models fail across contexts.

registers.title: Readiness overestimation & self-assessment optimism
registers.body: Management systematically overestimates readiness and underestimates complexity; single-assessor self-assessment carries hierarchy-correlated optimism bias.

registers.title: Spreading digital commitment too thin
registers.body: Breadth-first digitalization undermines returns; strategic attention is non-compensatory and must be focused.

registers.title: Governance restructuring as remedy
registers.body: Frequent governance redesign is a symptom of ineffectiveness, not a cure.

registers.title: Engineering participation
registers.body: Structured interventions alone cannot manufacture genuine employee participation; sentiment and needs determine it.

registers.title: Leaving decentralized IT covert
registers.body: Ungoverned shadow IT persists on misalignment; conversion to overt business-managed IT is the precondition for proportionate governance.

registers.title: Wholesale separation of digital activities
registers.body: Separating all digital activities (rather than exploration only) creates perceived injustice and starves the core of digital skills.

registers.title: Vertical-only EA adoption
registers.body: EA implemented only within limited departments caps enterprise-wide impact even in otherwise capable organizations.

registers.title: Maturity models without action linkage
registers.body: Assessing current-state maturity without barrier diagnosis or action conversion leaves transformation blocked.

registers.title: Top-down mandate vs bottom-up emergence
registers.body: Top-down technology-replication and strategy-driven EA compete with bottom-up process-diagnostic and initiative-driven adoption; evidence supports deliberate combination with trade-offs.

registers.title: Centralized standards vs decentralized autonomy
registers.body: Central standardization enables synergy but slows decisions and over-compromises; federated designs and risk-tiered guardrails are the resolution space.

registers.title: Agile autonomy vs architectural coherence
registers.body: Agile team autonomy conflicts with enterprise-level architectural coherence; integrator roles and coordination checkpoints mediate.

registers.title: Experimentation vs foundation stability
registers.body: Exploratory experimentation must be structurally protected from, and reconciled with, the stable operational core.

registers.title: Formal vs informal/relational governance
registers.body: Formal structures are easier to implement but relational mechanisms are necessary and differ in time-to-impact; soft governance is systematically under-measured.

registers.title: Separation vs integration of digital units
registers.body: Separate digital units accelerate early transformation but starve the core; maturity acts as the temporal trigger for re-integration.

registers.title: Disruptive vs evolutionary transformation modes
registers.body: Change culture bifurcates into radical reorientation versus failure-tolerant incrementalism as structurally distinct alternative paths; the evidence does not compare their effectiveness.
registers.notes: 2026-07-17 evidence amendment: removed contribution 115 (Sagala & Őri 2025; resilience versus antifragility) and the unrelated CC43 reference; remaining support 317/316 is Murawski et al. 2019; status remains proposed pending author closure.

registers.title: Stable governance design vs adaptive governance under disruption
registers.body: Durable, infrequently redesigned governance contrasts with adaptive committee cadence and priorities during disruption; resolution is adapting fundamentals rather than redesigning.

registers.title: Leadership perception vs frontline reality
registers.body: Leadership self-assessment of readiness, urgency, and soft-governance maturity systematically diverges from frontline perception and interview-corrected results.

registers.title: Transformation speed vs architectural feasibility
registers.body: Pace of change pressures pragmatic trade-offs between technically ideal and feasible architecture; coupling structure drives change cost.
